title: Physiology - Cardiovascular (DOMiNANCE Originals)
source: Built from CVS lecture slides (Circulation 1-3, Lectures 5-7)

questions.stem: The structures of the heart responsible for initiating and spreading the heartbeat make up the:
questions.why: The specialised conducting system consists of modified cardiac muscle cells that generate spontaneous impulses and distribute them through the atria and ventricles, coordinating the sequence of contraction.

notes.B: The fibrous skeleton supports the valves and electrically insulates the atria from the ventricles rather than generating the heartbeat.
notes.C: The coronary vascular network supplies oxygen and nutrients to the myocardium, including conducting cells, but does not conduct electrical impulses.
notes.D: The pericardial sac encloses the heart, limits excessive distension and reduces friction as the heart moves.
notes.E: Papillary muscles tense the chordae tendineae during ventricular contraction to prevent atrioventricular valve prolapse, not to initiate impulses.

questions.stem: In the terminology of the cardiac cycle, systole refers to:
questions.why: Systole is the phase of cardiac muscle contraction, during which the affected chamber develops pressure and may eject blood. Diastole is the corresponding relaxation phase.

notes.A: Valve opening depends on pressure differences and occurs during both ventricular ejection and filling, so it does not define systole.
notes.C: Relaxation is diastole, when ventricular pressure falls and eventually permits filling from the atria.
notes.D: Ventricular filling occurs mainly during diastole after ventricular pressure falls below atrial pressure, rather than during ventricular systole.
notes.E: Repolarisation restores the electrical membrane potential towards its resting value; it is an electrical event rather than the definition of mechanical contraction.

questions.stem: The resting cardiac output of the right ventricle compared with the left ventricle is:
questions.why: The pulmonary and systemic circulations are connected in series, so the two ventricles must pump approximately equal volumes per minute over time to prevent blood accumulating in either circulation.

notes.A: A persistently greater right ventricular output would deliver blood to the lungs faster than the left ventricle removes it, promoting pulmonary congestion.
notes.B: A persistently smaller right ventricular output would allow blood to accumulate on the systemic venous side and eventually reduce left ventricular filling.
notes.D: If the right ventricle pumped only half the left ventricular output, the imbalance could not persist without redistribution of blood and altered filling.
notes.E: A sustained twofold right ventricular output would overload the pulmonary circulation; the ventricles normally balance their average outputs despite different pressures.

questions.stem: The normal pacemaker of the heart is the:
questions.why: The sinoatrial node has the fastest intrinsic rate of spontaneous diastolic depolarisation among cardiac pacemaker tissues. It normally reaches threshold first and entrains the slower subsidiary pacemakers.

notes.A: The bundle of His conducts impulses across the fibrous cardiac skeleton and can provide a slower escape rhythm if higher pacemakers fail.
notes.B: Purkinje fibres rapidly distribute impulses through ventricular muscle and have slow latent automaticity, normally suppressed by the sinoatrial rhythm.
notes.C: Internodal pathways carry excitation through the atria towards the atrioventricular node; they do not normally determine the heart rate.
notes.E: The atrioventricular junction can generate a slower escape rhythm, typically 40–60 beats per minute, when sinoatrial impulses fail to arrive.

questions.stem: The sinoatrial node is located at the junction of the right atrium and the:
questions.why: The sinoatrial node lies subepicardially near the junction of the superior vena cava and right atrium, at the superior end of the sulcus terminalis.

notes.A: The inferior vena cava enters the lower right atrium; the sinoatrial node lies superiorly near the other caval opening.
notes.B: The coronary sinus opens into the inferior right atrium near the triangle of Koch, a landmark for the atrioventricular node.
notes.C: The pulmonary trunk arises from the right ventricle and carries blood to the lungs rather than joining the right atrium.
notes.D: The tricuspid valve guards the right atrioventricular opening; the sinoatrial node is situated higher in the right atrial wall.

questions.stem: The atrioventricular node is situated in the:

options.label: D
options.text: wall of the superior vena cava

questions.why: The atrioventricular node lies in the inferior interatrial septal region, within the triangle of Koch near the coronary sinus ostium and septal tricuspid annulus. It delays atrial impulses before ventricular activation.

notes.B: The anterior left atrial wall contains working atrial myocardium; the atrioventricular node is approached from the right atrial septal side.
notes.C: The left ventricular apex receives excitation through the distal Purkinje network and is far from the atrioventricular nodal region.
notes.D: The superior vena caval junction is a landmark for the sinoatrial node, not the more inferior atrioventricular node.
notes.E: The ventricular septal apex contains distal conduction fibres, whereas the atrioventricular node lies above the ventricular septum near the tricuspid annulus.

questions.stem: Which is the correct sequence of impulse conduction through the heart?

options.label: A
options.text: AV node, His, SA node, Purkinje fibres

options.label: B
options.text: SA node, AV node, bundle of His, Purkinje fibres

options.label: C
options.text: AV node, SA node, Purkinje fibres, His

options.label: D
options.text: SA node, His, AV node, Purkinje fibres

options.label: E
options.text: Purkinje fibres, His, AV node, SA node

questions.why: Excitation originates in the sinoatrial node, spreads through atrial myocardium and reaches the atrioventricular node. After nodal delay, the His bundle and bundle branches deliver it to the Purkinje network.

notes.A: This sequence starts in the atrioventricular node and places the sinoatrial node downstream of His, reversing the normal atrial initiation pathway.
notes.C: Normal excitation starts in the sinoatrial node, and the His bundle must activate before its distal Purkinje network.
notes.D: The atrioventricular node normally delays the impulse before it reaches the His bundle, not after transmission into the bundle.
notes.E: This sequence describes conduction in reverse; Purkinje fibres normally receive impulses from the bundle branches rather than initiating each heartbeat.

questions.stem: The anterior internodal tract connecting the atria to the AV node is also known as the tract of:
questions.why: In the classical description of atrial conduction, the anterior internodal pathway is associated with Bachmann, with an interatrial branch carrying excitation to the left atrium. Modern anatomy emphasises preferential conduction through atrial muscle.

notes.A: Purkinje fibres form the terminal ventricular conducting network and are not an anterior atrial internodal pathway.
notes.B: The bundle of His connects the atrioventricular node to the ventricular bundle branches rather than linking the sinoatrial and atrioventricular nodes.
notes.D: Wenckebach is associated with the middle internodal pathway in the classical description, not the anterior pathway.
notes.E: Thorel is associated with the posterior internodal pathway in the classical description, rather than the anterior route.

questions.stem: During normal diastole, the state of the heart valves is that the:

options.label: C
options.text: mitral and aortic valves are open

options.label: D
options.text: mitral and tricuspid valves are open

options.label: E
options.text: aortic and pulmonary valves are open

questions.why: In diastole the AV (mitral and tricuspid) valves are open and the semilunar valves closed, allowing filling.

questions.stem: What proportion of ventricular filling normally occurs passively, before atrial contraction?
questions.why: Most ventricular filling occurs passively after atrioventricular valves open, driven by the atrioventricular pressure gradient. In the lecture convention, about 70% is passive and atrial contraction contributes the remaining 30%.

notes.A: About 30% is the active atrial contribution in the stated teaching convention, not the predominant passive component.
notes.B: Half of filling would overestimate the usual dependence on atrial contraction in a healthy resting heart.
notes.C: Ten per cent substantially underestimates the passive filling that occurs before atrial contraction in normal resting physiology.
notes.D: Passive filling can vary with heart rate and compliance, but 90% exceeds the usual approximate teaching value of 70–80%.

questions.stem: The phase in which the ventricle contracts with all valves closed and no change in volume is:
questions.why: During isovolumetric contraction, ventricular pressure rises after atrioventricular valve closure but before semilunar valve opening. With no inlet or outlet open, ventricular volume remains constant at end-diastolic volume.

notes.B: Rapid ejection begins when ventricular pressure exceeds arterial pressure and opens the semilunar valves, allowing ventricular volume to fall.
notes.C: Isovolumetric relaxation also occurs with all valves closed, but ventricular pressure falls rather than rising as the myocardium relaxes.
notes.D: Rapid filling follows atrioventricular valve opening and increases ventricular volume as blood enters from the atria.
notes.E: Atrial systole increases ventricular filling through open atrioventricular valves, rather than raising ventricular pressure at constant volume.

questions.stem: The left ventricular pressure must exceed roughly what value before the aortic valve opens?
questions.why: The aortic valve opens when left ventricular pressure exceeds the pressure in the aortic root, which at end-diastole is approximately 80 mmHg in a normotensive adult.

notes.A: Around 25 mmHg is closer to normal peak right ventricular systolic pressure, far below the usual aortic opening pressure.
notes.C: Around 10 mmHg may approximate left ventricular end-diastolic pressure but is insufficient to overcome normal aortic diastolic pressure.
notes.D: About 120 mmHg is typical peak left ventricular systolic pressure reached during ejection, after the aortic valve has opened.
notes.E: A pressure of 40 mmHg remains below typical aortic diastolic pressure, so the valve would normally remain closed.

questions.stem: The end-diastolic ventricular volume is approximately:
questions.why: End-diastolic volume is the amount of blood in a ventricle immediately before systole, after passive filling and atrial contraction. A typical teaching value is about 120–130 mL.

notes.A: A volume of 200 mL exceeds the usual resting end-diastolic volume and may occur with marked ventricular dilatation or increased filling.
notes.B: A volume of 90 mL is lower than the standard resting end-diastolic teaching value and closer to a large resting stroke volume.
notes.D: Approximately 70 mL is a typical resting stroke volume, the amount expelled rather than the total volume before contraction.
notes.E: Approximately 50 mL is a typical end-systolic residual volume left in the ventricle after ejection, not the filled volume.

questions.stem: The stroke volume, the amount ejected per beat, is normally about:
questions.why: Stroke volume equals end-diastolic volume minus end-systolic volume. A ventricle containing about 130 mL before contraction and 50 mL afterwards ejects approximately 80 mL per beat.

notes.A: A volume of 130–150 mL is closer to normal end-diastolic volume, not the amount normally ejected at rest.
notes.B: A volume of 40–50 mL is closer to a typical end-systolic volume and would represent a relatively low resting stroke volume.
notes.C: A stroke volume of 100–120 mL can occur with increased filling or exercise but exceeds the usual resting teaching range.
notes.E: A stroke volume of 10–20 mL would be markedly reduced for an adult and is not typical of normal resting cardiac function.

questions.stem: The ejection fraction of a normal ventricle is approximately:
questions.why: Ejection fraction is stroke volume divided by end-diastolic volume, expressed as a percentage. A ventricle ejecting around 80 mL from 125 mL has an ejection fraction of approximately 64%.

notes.A: An ejection fraction of 100% would require complete ventricular emptying, whereas a normal ventricle retains blood after systole.
notes.B: An ejection fraction around 40% indicates reduced left ventricular systolic function rather than normal resting emptying.
notes.C: An ejection fraction of 85% exceeds the usual normal resting range and may reflect a small hyperdynamic ventricle.
notes.D: An ejection fraction of 25% indicates severely reduced systolic emptying, not the normal proportion of end-diastolic blood ejected.

questions.stem: The brief interval after full contraction, during which ventricular pressure begins to fall and ends with closure of the semilunar valves, is called:
questions.why: Protodiastole is the brief transitional period at the end of ventricular ejection when ventricular pressure falls and forward flow decelerates. Semilunar valve closure marks its end.

notes.B: Isovolumetric relaxation begins after semilunar valve closure, so it follows rather than describes the protodiastolic interval.
notes.C: Rapid ejection occurs earlier in systole, when ventricular contraction drives brisk blood flow through open semilunar valves.
notes.D: Reduced filling occurs later in diastole, after atrioventricular valves open and the initial rapid filling phase slows.
notes.E: Atrial systole occurs near the end of ventricular diastole and augments filling before the next ventricular contraction.

questions.stem: According to Starling's law of the heart, the force of contraction is proportional to the:

options.label: B
options.text: initial length of the muscle fibre

options.label: D
options.text: prevailing heart rate at the time

questions.why: The Frank–Starling mechanism increases the force developed by cardiac muscle when its initial fibre length increases within the physiological range. Greater filling therefore normally increases stroke volume without increased intrinsic contractility.

notes.A: Ventricular wall thickness influences wall stress and pressure-generating capacity, but it is not the length-dependent variable in the Frank–Starling relationship.
notes.C: Afterload opposes ventricular ejection and can alter stroke volume, but the Frank–Starling law specifically concerns initial myocardial fibre length.
notes.D: Heart rate affects filling time and cardiac output; the Frank–Starling mechanism links contraction strength to initial stretch rather than pacing rate.
notes.E: Adrenaline increases contractility at a given fibre length through adrenergic signalling, which is distinct from length-dependent Frank–Starling regulation.

questions.stem: Preload is best defined as the:

options.label: C
options.text: degree of myocardial stretch before contraction

options.label: D
options.text: resistance against which blood is expelled

questions.why: Preload describes myocardial fibre stretch immediately before contraction, commonly approximated clinically by ventricular end-diastolic volume or pressure. Increased preload normally increases contraction force through the Frank–Starling mechanism.

notes.A: The rate of ventricular relaxation is a lusitropic property that influences filling but does not itself define the initial fibre stretch.
notes.B: The volume ejected per beat is stroke volume, which is an outcome affected by preload, afterload and contractility.
notes.D: Resistance opposing ventricular ejection describes afterload, a mechanical load during contraction rather than stretch before contraction.
notes.E: The force developed during contraction depends partly on preload and intrinsic contractility, but preload refers to the preceding stretch.

questions.stem: Afterload on the left ventricle corresponds most closely to the:

options.label: A
options.text: the venous return reaching the heart

options.label: B
options.text: the intrinsic rate of the pacemaker

options.label: E
options.text: the degree of diastolic stretch applied

questions.why: Left ventricular afterload is the load opposing myocardial shortening during ejection. It depends largely on aortic pressure and ventricular wall stress, with arterial resistance and compliance influencing that pressure.

notes.A: Venous return supplies ventricular filling and therefore influences preload, rather than directly defining the load opposing left ventricular ejection.
notes.B: The intrinsic pacemaker rate determines the frequency of spontaneous cardiac excitation, not the mechanical load against which the ventricle contracts.
notes.C: End-diastolic muscle fibre length represents initial myocardial stretch and is related to preload rather than afterload.
notes.E: Diastolic stretch describes preload established before ventricular contraction, not the arterial load opposing blood ejection.

questions.stem: Regulation of cardiac output by changes in muscle fibre length is termed:
questions.why: Heterometric regulation adjusts contraction force through changes in initial myocardial fibre length, as in the Frank–Starling mechanism. Homometric regulation changes contractility without requiring an increase in fibre length.

notes.A: Homometric regulation changes force at a given initial fibre length, rather than using altered filling and fibre stretch.
notes.B: Chronotropic regulation alters heart rate and can influence cardiac output, but does not specifically describe length-dependent changes in force.
notes.C: Autoregulation is a broader term for intrinsic regulation and does not identify the specific length-dependent mechanism requested.
notes.D: Neural regulation uses autonomic input to alter cardiac performance, whereas heterometric regulation is an intrinsic response to initial fibre stretch.

questions.stem: A change in the strength of cardiac contraction, independent of fibre length, is called a(n):
questions.why: An inotropic effect changes intrinsic myocardial contractility at a given initial fibre length and loading condition. Positive inotropy increases force development, as occurs with sympathetic stimulation.

notes.B: A chronotropic effect changes the rate of cardiac impulse generation rather than directly describing myocardial contractile strength.
notes.C: A dromotropic effect changes conduction velocity, especially through the atrioventricular node, rather than the force of contraction.
notes.D: A bathmotropic effect changes myocardial excitability or the ease with which an action potential is triggered, not intrinsic contractile strength.
notes.E: A lusitropic effect changes myocardial relaxation, influencing diastolic filling rather than defining systolic contractile force.

questions.stem: Catecholamines increase myocardial contractility mainly by acting on which receptors?
questions.why: Cardiac beta-1 adrenergic receptors activate Gs proteins, adenylyl cyclase and the cAMP–protein kinase A pathway. Increased calcium entry and sarcoplasmic reticulum calcium release strengthen contraction.

notes.A: Nicotinic receptors mediate cholinergic transmission in autonomic ganglia but are not the main myocardial receptors for catecholamine-induced inotropy.
notes.C: Alpha-1 receptors mainly mediate vascular smooth muscle contraction, although cardiac alpha-1 signalling can contribute to inotropy in some circumstances.
notes.D: Cardiac muscarinic M2 receptors mediate parasympathetic signalling and tend to reduce cAMP and nodal activity rather than mediate sympathetic positive inotropy.
notes.E: Beta-2 receptors can contribute to cardiac responses and mediate smooth muscle relaxation, but beta-1 receptors predominate in the normal myocardial response.

questions.stem: Caffeine and theophylline increase cardiac contractility because they:
questions.why: Methylxanthines such as theophylline can inhibit phosphodiesterases, decreasing cAMP breakdown and enhancing calcium-dependent contractility. Adenosine receptor antagonism also contributes to methylxanthine cardiac effects, particularly at lower concentrations.

notes.A: Reducing calcium entry generally weakens cardiac contraction because less trigger calcium is available for sarcoplasmic reticulum calcium release.
notes.B: Depleting catecholamines would reduce adrenergic stimulation rather than explain the positive inotropic effect of methylxanthines.
notes.D: Blocking beta-1 receptors reduces adrenergic cAMP production and generally decreases contractility rather than producing the stated positive inotropic response.
notes.E: Vagal stimulation predominantly slows nodal activity and can reduce atrial contractility, rather than explaining methylxanthine-induced increases in contraction force.

questions.stem: It is impossible to tetanise cardiac muscle because of its:
questions.why: The prolonged cardiac action potential, particularly its calcium-dependent plateau, produces a refractory period that overlaps most of the contraction. A second effective excitation cannot arrive early enough for sustained tetanic summation.

notes.A: Cardiac muscle receives autonomic innervation, although its intrinsic pacemaker activity does not depend on nerves; innervation does not explain the absence of tetany.
notes.B: Abundant mitochondria provide ATP for continuous aerobic cardiac work, but do not determine the electrical refractory period preventing tetanic summation.
notes.C: Calcium entry during the plateau contributes to contraction and action potential duration, but a continuous pathological calcium leak is not the normal anti-tetany mechanism.
notes.E: Cardiomyocytes are relatively small branched cells, but cell size does not prevent repeated excitation during a prolonged refractory period.

questions.stem: On the electrocardiogram, the P wave represents:
questions.why: The P wave records the summed electrical activity of atrial depolarisation as excitation spreads from the sinoatrial region through both atria. Atrial mechanical contraction follows this electrical event.

notes.A: Ventricular depolarisation generates the QRS complex because the large ventricular muscle mass produces a prominent electrical deflection.
notes.B: Ventricular repolarisation generates the T wave, which occurs after ventricular depolarisation rather than before ventricular activation.
notes.C: Atrial repolarisation usually overlaps the QRS complex and is obscured by the much larger ventricular electrical signal.
notes.D: The ventricular action potential plateau corresponds broadly to the ST segment, when most ventricular muscle remains depolarised.

questions.stem: The QRS complex of the ECG represents:
questions.why: The QRS complex represents the spread of depolarisation through the ventricles via the His–Purkinje system and ventricular myocardium. Its electrical activation precedes the development of ventricular contraction.

notes.B: Atrial depolarisation produces the P wave before ventricular activation, rather than the larger QRS deflection.
notes.C: Ventricular repolarisation produces the T wave as ventricular muscle returns towards its resting electrical state.
notes.D: Atrial repolarisation is usually concealed within the QRS complex but is not the principal electrical event generating that complex.
notes.E: Atrioventricular nodal delay contributes to the PR interval and segment before ventricular depolarisation begins.

questions.stem: The normal PR interval ranges from:
questions.why: The PR interval extends from the onset of the P wave to the onset of the QRS complex. Normally 0.12–0.20 seconds, it includes atrial conduction and atrioventricular conduction delay.

notes.A: A PR interval of 0.40–0.60 seconds would be markedly prolonged and could indicate severe atrioventricular conduction delay.
notes.C: A PR interval of 0.06–0.10 seconds is abnormally short for an adult and may suggest pre-excitation or an abnormal atrial origin.
notes.D: Values above 0.20 seconds represent prolonged atrioventricular conduction; the proposed range extends well beyond the normal upper limit.
notes.E: An interval of 0.02–0.08 seconds is too short to account for normal atrial activation and atrioventricular conduction delay.

questions.stem: The T wave of the electrocardiogram corresponds to:
questions.why: The T wave reflects ventricular repolarisation, as ventricular myocytes restore their resting membrane potential after the action potential plateau. Its direction depends on the sequence of repolarisation.

notes.A: Atrial depolarisation produces the P wave before the QRS complex, not the later T wave.
notes.B: Atrioventricular conduction is reflected mainly in the PR interval between atrial and ventricular activation, not the T wave.
notes.D: Ventricular depolarisation produces the QRS complex, preceding the ST segment and subsequent ventricular repolarisation.
notes.E: Atrial repolarisation is usually hidden by the QRS complex and does not generate the normal T wave.

questions.stem: ST-segment depression or elevation is important in the diagnosis of:
questions.why: Myocardial ischaemia alters ventricular action potentials and creates regional electrical potential differences that may shift the ST segment. ST elevation or depression can support an ischaemic diagnosis when interpreted with symptoms and other ECG findings.

notes.A: First-degree atrioventricular block is identified by a prolonged PR interval, not primarily by ST-segment displacement.
notes.B: Bundle branch block primarily widens and changes QRS morphology; secondary ST-T changes may occur but are not its defining finding.
notes.C: Sinus arrhythmia changes successive RR intervals with preserved sinus activation rather than primarily shifting the ST segment.
notes.E: Atrial enlargement alters P-wave amplitude or duration, whereas ischaemic ST changes reflect altered ventricular electrical behaviour.

questions.stem: On standard ECG paper, one small (1 mm) square represents how much time?
questions.why: At the standard ECG recording speed of 25 mm per second, each 1 mm horizontal division represents 1/25 second, or 0.04 seconds. Five small squares equal 0.20 seconds.

notes.A: At 25 mm per second, 0.10 seconds spans 2.5 small horizontal squares rather than a single division.
notes.B: A duration of 0.20 seconds corresponds to one large 5 mm square at standard recording speed, not one small square.
notes.C: A single small square represents 0.02 seconds at 50 mm per second, not at the specified standard speed.
notes.D: A duration of 0.01 seconds would require 100 mm per second for each millimetre, rather than standard ECG paper speed.

questions.stem: Heart rate can be estimated by dividing which number by the number of large squares between two R waves?
questions.why: Rate = 300/large squares (or 1500/small squares) between successive R waves.

questions.stem: The first heart sound is produced by closure of the:
questions.why: S1 is the near-simultaneous closure of the mitral and tricuspid (AV) valves at the start of systole.

questions.stem: The second heart sound marks the:
questions.why: S2 (closure of the semilunar valves) occurs at the end of systole/beginning of diastole.

questions.stem: Physiological splitting of the second heart sound during inspiration occurs because the:

options.label: C
options.text: aortic and pulmonary valves close together

options.label: D
options.text: aortic valve closes before the pulmonary valve

options.label: E
options.text: pulmonary valve closes before the aortic valve

questions.why: Inspiration increases venous return and prolongs right ventricular ejection, so the pulmonary valve closes after the aortic.

questions.stem: A third heart sound in diastole, when present, is due to:

options.label: B
options.text: atrial contraction against a closed valve

options.label: C
options.text: turbulent flow across a stenosed valve

questions.why: S3 results from rapid passive ventricular filling in early diastole.

questions.stem: A heart murmur is generally caused by:
questions.why: Murmurs arise from turbulent (non-laminar) flow, as across abnormal valves or in hyperdynamic circulation.

questions.stem: The arterial pulse that can be palpated is produced by:

options.label: B
options.text: a pressure wave expanding the arterial wall

options.label: C
options.text: the actual velocity of the blood column

questions.why: The pulse is a pressure wave travelling along the arteries, felt as expansion of the wall - independent of blood velocity.

questions.stem: As a person ages, the arterial pulse wave travels:

options.label: A
options.text: faster, because the heart rate rises

options.label: B
options.text: slower, because blood becomes more viscous

options.label: C
options.text: faster, because arteries become more rigid

options.label: D
options.text: slower, because arteries become more elastic

questions.why: Stiffer (less elastic) arteries with age transmit the pressure wave faster.

questions.stem: The 'a' wave of the jugular venous pulse is produced by:
questions.why: The 'a' wave reflects atrial contraction causing a brief rise in venous pressure.

questions.stem: A giant 'a' wave in the jugular venous pulse is characteristically seen in:
questions.why: In heart block the atrium contracts against a closed tricuspid valve, producing a giant 'a' wave.

questions.stem: Cardiac output is correctly expressed as:
questions.why: Cardiac output = heart rate x stroke volume.

questions.stem: The cardiac index is the cardiac output expressed per unit of:
questions.why: Cardiac index is cardiac output divided by body surface area.

questions.stem: Vagal (parasympathetic) stimulation of the heart produces a:
questions.why: Vagal stimulation slows the heart (negative chronotropy) and is also negatively inotropic.

questions.stem: Which of the following would INCREASE end-diastolic volume (and thus stroke volume by Starling's law)?
questions.why: Increased venous tone raises venous return and end-diastolic volume; the other options reduce filling.

questions.stem: Which factor would DECREASE end-diastolic volume?
questions.why: Gravitational pooling on standing reduces venous return and end-diastolic volume.

questions.stem: During exercise, cardiac output rises partly because afterload falls as a result of:
questions.why: Exercise causes vasodilatation in active muscle, lowering peripheral resistance and afterload.

questions.stem: Which of the following depresses myocardial contractility?
questions.why: Hypercapnia, hypoxia and acidosis depress contractility; catecholamines and xanthines increase it.

questions.stem: The Fick principle measures cardiac output using oxygen as the indicator; output equals oxygen consumption divided by the:
questions.why: By Fick, blood flow = O2 consumption / (arterial - venous O2 difference).

questions.stem: For the Fick principle applied to the whole body, the true mixed venous oxygen sample is taken from the:
questions.why: Mixed venous blood for the Fick calculation is sampled from the pulmonary artery.

questions.stem: The central venous pressure, measured at the entrance to the right atrium, is normally about:
questions.why: Peripheral venous pressure is ~12-18 mmHg, falling to about 4-6 mmHg (CVP) at the right atrium.

questions.stem: Which mechanism helps return venous blood to the heart?
questions.why: The skeletal muscle pump (with venous valves and the thoracic pump) aids venous return.

questions.stem: Veins are described as capacitance vessels because they:

options.label: B
options.text: hold a large reserve volume at low pressure

options.label: C
options.text: provide the main resistance to flow

questions.why: Veins accommodate large volumes with little pressure change, acting as the blood reservoir.

questions.stem: Heart failure is best defined as a state in which the heart cannot meet the metabolic needs of the tissues despite:

options.label: C
options.text: a normal or increased venous return

questions.why: In heart failure the pump fails even though venous return is normal or raised.

questions.stem: Backward failure of the LEFT heart characteristically produces:
questions.why: Left-sided backward failure raises pulmonary capillary pressure, causing pulmonary oedema and dyspnoea.

questions.stem: Backward failure of the RIGHT heart characteristically produces:
questions.why: Right-sided backward failure raises systemic venous pressure, causing peripheral oedema, hepatomegaly and ascites.

questions.stem: Forward failure of the left heart mainly causes symptoms of:
questions.why: Forward failure reflects inadequate output, giving fatigue, weakness and oliguria from hypoperfusion.

questions.stem: According to the Poiseuille-Hagen relationship, the resistance to blood flow is inversely proportional to the:
questions.why: Resistance = 8Ln/(pi r^4), so it varies as 1/r^4 - radius is the dominant factor.

questions.stem: Halving the radius of a vessel, with all else constant, changes its resistance by a factor of:
questions.why: Because resistance varies as 1/r^4, halving the radius multiplies resistance by 2^4 = 16.

questions.stem: Blood flow through a vessel is directly proportional to the:
questions.why: Flow = pressure difference / resistance, so flow rises with the perfusion pressure gradient.

questions.stem: The chief determinant of resistance to blood flow in the circulation is the:
questions.why: Vessel radius (regulated by smooth muscle) is the main controllable determinant of resistance.

questions.stem: Turbulent blood flow, unlike laminar flow, is characterised by:
questions.why: Turbulence creates noise (bruits, Korotkoff sounds); laminar flow is silent.

questions.stem: A high Reynolds number, favouring turbulent flow, is promoted by:
questions.why: Reynolds number rises with velocity, diameter and density and falls with viscosity; high values mean turbulence.

questions.stem: Blood velocity is highest in the aorta and lowest in the capillaries because the capillaries have the:
questions.why: Velocity = flow/area; the huge combined cross-section of capillaries makes velocity lowest there.

questions.stem: Blood viscosity depends chiefly on the:
questions.why: Viscosity rises mainly with haematocrit (as in polycythaemia) and falls in anaemia.

questions.stem: Autoregulation of blood flow is the capacity of a tissue to:

options.label: E
options.text: keep its own blood flow nearly constant

questions.why: Autoregulation keeps local flow relatively constant by adjusting vascular resistance when perfusion pressure changes.

questions.stem: By the metabolic theory of autoregulation, a fall in local blood flow leads to:
questions.why: Reduced flow lets vasodilator metabolites accumulate, dilating vessels and restoring flow.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a local metabolic VASODILATOR?
questions.why: Adenosine, CO2, H+, K+, lactate and low O2 dilate; serotonin, angiotensin and cold constrict.

questions.stem: Endothelium-derived relaxing factor, which mediates vasodilatation by substances such as bradykinin, is:
questions.why: EDRF is nitric oxide, produced by endothelium to relax vascular smooth muscle.

questions.stem: The myogenic theory of autoregulation holds that vascular smooth muscle contracts in response to:

options.label: A
options.text: a fall in the oxygen tension

questions.why: By the myogenic theory, raised distending pressure stretches and reflexly contracts the smooth muscle.

questions.stem: By the law of Laplace, for a given wall tension the distending pressure a vessel can withstand is greater when its radius is:
questions.why: Laplace (P = T/r for a cylinder): a smaller radius means a higher pressure is tolerated for the same tension.

questions.stem: Pulse pressure is defined as the:

options.label: A
options.text: difference between systolic and diastolic pressure

options.label: C
options.text: diastolic pressure plus one-third of systolic

options.label: E
options.text: sum of systolic and diastolic pressure

questions.why: Pulse pressure = systolic minus diastolic pressure.

questions.stem: Mean arterial pressure is estimated as:

options.label: B
options.text: diastolic pressure plus one-third of the pulse pressure

options.label: C
options.text: the average of systolic and diastolic pressure

options.label: E
options.text: diastolic pressure plus the pulse pressure

questions.why: MAP is approximated as diastolic + 1/3 (pulse pressure) because diastole lasts longer.

questions.stem: Maintenance of arterial pressure during diastole, by elastic recoil of the large arteries, is known as the:
questions.why: The elastic recoil of the aorta sustaining diastolic flow is the Windkessel effect.

questions.stem: The first Korotkoff sound heard while deflating a blood-pressure cuff corresponds to the:
questions.why: The first Korotkoff (tapping) sound marks systolic pressure; disappearance marks diastolic.

questions.stem: Using a cuff that is too SMALL for the arm gives a reading that is falsely:
questions.why: A too-small cuff reads falsely high; a too-large cuff reads falsely low.

questions.stem: When measuring blood pressure, the cuff must be positioned at the level of the:
questions.why: The cuff should be at heart level, or gravity distorts the reading.

questions.stem: The main integrating centre controlling arteriolar tone and blood pressure is located in the:
questions.why: The vasomotor centre of the medulla oblongata is the principal controller of vascular tone and BP.

questions.stem: Blood vessels receive a continuous (tonic) discharge from which fibres?
questions.why: There is tonic sympathetic vasoconstrictor discharge; reducing it causes vasodilatation.

questions.stem: Sympathetic vasodilator fibres to vessels in skeletal muscle are unusual in that they are:
questions.why: Sympathetic vasodilator fibres (to muscle and liver) release acetylcholine - they are cholinergic.

questions.stem: Sympathetic stimulation of the heart produces a:

options.label: B
options.text: rise in rate but fall in force

options.label: C
options.text: fall in rate but rise in force

options.label: D
options.text: no change in rate or force

options.label: E
options.text: rise in both rate and force

questions.why: Sympathetic activity increases both heart rate (chronotropy) and strength of contraction (inotropy).

questions.stem: Resting heart rate is held down mainly by:

options.label: D
options.text: the intrinsic SA node rate alone

questions.why: Tonic vagal tone keeps resting rate below the intrinsic SA rate; vagotomy or atropine raises the rate.

questions.stem: Atrial natriuretic peptide acts on the vasculature to cause:
questions.why: ANP is a vasodilator (and promotes sodium/water loss).

questions.stem: The arterial baroreceptors are located in the carotid sinus and the:
questions.why: High-pressure baroreceptors lie in the carotid sinus and the aortic arch.

questions.stem: Afferent impulses from the carotid sinus baroreceptors travel to the medulla in the:
questions.why: Carotid sinus afferents run in the carotid sinus nerve, a branch of the glossopharyngeal; aortic afferents run in the vagus.

questions.stem: A sudden RISE in arterial pressure triggers a baroreceptor reflex that causes:

options.label: A
options.text: speeding of the heart and vasoconstriction

options.label: E
options.text: slowing of the heart and vasodilatation

questions.why: Raised pressure increases baroreceptor firing, stimulating the vagus and inhibiting the vasomotor centre, so the heart slows and vessels dilate.

questions.stem: A FALL in arterial pressure produces a reflex that leads to:
questions.why: Reduced baroreceptor firing raises sympathetic output and reduces vagal tone, giving tachycardia and vasoconstriction.

questions.stem: The Cushing reflex, triggered by raised intracranial pressure, classically produces:

options.label: A
options.text: no change in pressure or rate

questions.why: Raised intracranial pressure causes systemic hypertension, and the baroreceptors then produce reflex bradycardia.

questions.stem: The vasomotor centre is directly stimulated by:
questions.why: Hypoxia and hypercapnia directly excite the vasomotor centre, raising sympathetic output.

questions.stem: On standing, blood tends to pool in the dependent veins; the resulting fall in arterial pressure is sensed by the:

options.label: D
options.text: aortic arch and carotid sinus receptors

questions.why: The pressure drop above heart level is detected by the carotid sinus and aortic arch baroreceptors, triggering compensation.

questions.stem: Orthostatic (postural) hypotension is characteristically due to failure of:
questions.why: When sympathetic vasoconstriction fails (e.g. autonomic neuropathy, sympatholytic drugs), standing causes a fall in BP.

questions.stem: During exposure to high positive (+Gz) acceleration, loss of vision ('black-out') occurs because of:
questions.why: Positive g drives blood footward, reducing cerebral perfusion so that vision fails and consciousness is lost.

questions.stem: A pressure ('g') suit improves tolerance to acceleration by:

options.label: B
options.text: compressing the legs to limit pooling

questions.why: The suit compresses the lower body, reducing venous pooling and improving venous return.

questions.stem: Circulatory shock is best defined as:

options.label: B
options.text: loss of consciousness from any cause

options.label: D
options.text: a sustained rise in arterial pressure

questions.why: Shock is inadequate tissue perfusion for metabolic/nutritional needs, with a relative or absolute low output.

questions.stem: Shock due to haemorrhage, burns or severe vomiting is classified as:
questions.why: Loss of circulating volume (haemorrhage, burns, fluid loss) gives hypovolaemic shock.

questions.stem: Shock caused by cardiac tamponade or massive pulmonary embolism is classified as:
questions.why: A physical obstruction to flow (tamponade, tension pneumothorax, pulmonary embolism) causes obstructive shock.

questions.stem: In early hypovolaemic shock the skin is typically pale and cool because of:

options.label: C
options.text: a rise in the cardiac output

questions.why: Baroreceptor-driven sympathetic discharge constricts skin vessels, making the skin pale and cool.

questions.stem: During shock, blood flow is preferentially preserved to the:
questions.why: Generalised vasoconstriction spares the coronary and cerebral circulations while diverting blood from skin, kidney and viscera.

questions.stem: Distributive (low-resistance) shock, such as septic or anaphylactic shock, is characterised by:
questions.why: Distributive shock has a normal volume but massive vasodilatation and pooling, so perfusion is inadequate.

questions.stem: Vasovagal syncope (simple fainting) is caused by:
questions.why: Fainting follows abrupt vasodilatation and bradycardia after strong emotion, reducing cerebral blood flow.

questions.stem: The wall of a typical capillary consists of:

options.label: E
options.text: a single layer of endothelial cells

questions.why: Capillaries have a wall one endothelial cell thick, allowing exchange.

questions.stem: Blood flow into a capillary bed is controlled by:
questions.why: Precapillary sphincters (smooth muscle, responding to local substances rather than nerves) regulate capillary flow.

questions.stem: Fenestrations in capillary endothelium, allowing passage of larger molecules, are especially prominent in the:
questions.why: Fenestrated capillaries occur where exchange is high - kidney, intestinal villi and endocrine glands; brain capillaries are non-fenestrated.

questions.stem: According to Starling's forces, the main pressure driving fluid OUT of the capillary is the:
questions.why: Capillary hydrostatic pressure drives filtration out; plasma oncotic pressure draws fluid back in.

questions.stem: Of the fluid filtered out of the capillaries each day, the proportion returned to the circulation by the lymphatics is about:
questions.why: About 85% of filtered fluid is reabsorbed by capillaries and roughly 15% is returned via lymph.

questions.stem: Oedema is an abnormal accumulation of fluid in the:
questions.why: Oedema is excess fluid in the interstitium, from increased filtration or inadequate reabsorption/drainage.

questions.stem: A fall in plasma protein concentration (as in liver disease, nephrotic syndrome or malnutrition) causes oedema by:

options.label: A
options.text: lowering the plasma colloid osmotic pressure

questions.why: Low plasma proteins reduce the oncotic pull back into capillaries, so fluid stays in the interstitium.

questions.stem: Non-pitting oedema (lymphoedema), as in elephantiasis after filarial infection, is caused by:
questions.why: Lymphatic obstruction (e.g. filarial worms, radical mastectomy) causes protein-rich, non-pitting lymphoedema.

questions.stem: The lymphatic vessels ultimately return lymph to the bloodstream at the:

options.label: E
options.text: the right atrium of the heart

questions.why: Lymph drains into the venous system at the subclavian veins (right and left).

questions.stem: Lymph flow along the vessels is aided by all of the following EXCEPT:

options.label: B
options.text: rhythmic contractions of the vessel wall

options.label: D
options.text: direct pumping of lymph by the heart

questions.why: Lymph is moved by the muscle pump, thoracic pump, wall contractions and valves - not by direct cardiac pumping.

questions.stem: An important function of the lymphatic system is the:

options.label: C
options.text: production of the red blood cells

options.label: E
options.text: returning filtered protein to the blood

questions.why: Lymphatics return filtered interstitial protein (and absorbed fat) to the blood.

questions.stem: The coronary arteries arise from the:
questions.why: The right and left coronary arteries arise from the aortic sinuses behind the aortic valve cusps.

questions.stem: Coronary blood flow to the left ventricular myocardium occurs mainly during:
questions.why: During systole the intramural vessels are compressed, so left ventricular coronary flow occurs chiefly in diastole.

questions.stem: Angina pectoris on exertion typically occurs when a coronary artery is narrowed by about:
questions.why: Flow is adequate at rest but inadequate on exertion once a vessel is ~75% occluded, causing angina.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a potent metabolic coronary VASODILATOR?
questions.why: Adenosine (with O2 lack, K+, H+, CO2, lactate) dilates coronary vessels during increased cardiac work.

questions.stem: The arterial anastomosis at the base of the brain is the:
questions.why: The circle of Willis links the internal carotid and vertebrobasilar supplies at the brain's base.

questions.stem: Cerebrospinal fluid is produced mainly by the:
questions.why: CSF is secreted mainly by the choroid plexuses of the lateral, third and fourth ventricles.

questions.stem: Cerebrospinal fluid is absorbed back into the venous blood through the:
questions.why: CSF passes into the subarachnoid space and is absorbed through the arachnoid villi into the dural sinuses.

questions.stem: The Monro-Kellie doctrine states that the sum of the volumes of brain, CSF and which other component is constant within the rigid skull?
questions.why: The cranial contents - brain, CSF and blood - have a near-constant total volume (Monro-Kellie doctrine).

questions.stem: The blood-brain barrier allows easy passage of:
questions.why: Small, lipid-soluble, non-polar molecules cross easily; proteins and protein-bound substances do not.

questions.stem: An ischaemic stroke is most often caused by:

options.label: B
options.text: a fall in the CSF pressure

options.label: D
options.text: a rise in the venous pressure

options.label: E
options.text: a thrombus or embolus in an artery

questions.why: Ischaemic stroke results from arterial occlusion (atherosclerotic thrombus or embolus); haemorrhagic stroke from vessel rupture.

questions.stem: Compared with the systemic circulation, the pulmonary circulation is a:
questions.why: The pulmonary circulation operates at low pressure (~10 mmHg capillary) and low resistance.

questions.stem: In the lung, alveolar hypoxia causes the local pulmonary vessels to:
questions.why: Hypoxic pulmonary vasoconstriction diverts blood from poorly ventilated areas to better-oxygenated ones.

questions.stem: The low hydrostatic pressure in pulmonary capillaries is important because it:

options.label: C
options.text: keeps fluid from accumulating in the alveoli

options.label: D
options.text: raises the work of the right heart

questions.why: Low pulmonary capillary pressure (below plasma oncotic pressure) keeps the alveoli dry.

questions.stem: On lying down, the volume of blood held in the lungs:
questions.why: The lungs act as a blood reservoir; lying down adds about 400 ml to the pulmonary circulation.

questions.stem: The three unpaired arteries supplying the splanchnic (gut) circulation are the celiac trunk, the superior mesenteric artery and the:
questions.why: The gut is supplied by the celiac trunk and the superior and inferior mesenteric arteries.

questions.stem: During shock or heavy sympathetic discharge, the splanchnic circulation characteristically:

options.label: A
options.text: constricts and releases its stored blood

options.label: B
options.text: dilates further to store more blood

questions.why: The splanchnic bed is a large venous reservoir; in shock it constricts and shifts blood to the vital circulations.

questions.stem: Within the liver lobule, blood flows from the portal triad towards the:
questions.why: Blood flows from the triad through the sinusoids to the central vein; the perivenous zone is least oxygenated.

questions.stem: In the formation of ascites, the protein-rich fluid leaking from the liver is explained by the fact that hepatic sinusoids:

options.label: C
options.text: have pores permeable to plasma protein

questions.why: Sinusoidal pores let protein into the space of Disse; raised hepatic venous pressure then drives protein-rich fluid out as ascites.

questions.stem: The main physiological role of the cutaneous circulation is:
questions.why: Skin blood flow, with its many anastomoses, is primarily for heat exchange and thermoregulation.

questions.stem: In the triple response of the skin, the spreading redness ('flare') around an injury is due to:

options.label: E
options.text: arteriolar dilatation via an axon reflex

questions.why: The flare is arteriolar dilatation spreading by an antidromic axon reflex; the wheal is local oedema from increased permeability.

questions.stem: The initial 'white reaction' after lightly stroking the skin is caused by:
questions.why: Light stroking contracts precapillary sphincters, draining the capillaries and producing pallor for ~15 s.

questions.stem: Fetal haemoglobin binds oxygen more avidly than adult haemoglobin because it has a:
questions.why: HbF binds 2,3-DPG poorly, so its oxygen affinity is higher than maternal HbA, favouring placental O2 uptake.

questions.stem: Fetal haemoglobin is normally largely replaced by adult haemoglobin by about:
questions.why: HbF usually disappears by around 4 months after birth as HbA predominates.
